articles.title: Trump says suspension of Russia sanctions is to keep peace negotiations going
articles.summary: The US president blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect.
body: US President Donald Trump has said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table.

"I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine," Trump said on his Truth Social messaging platform, adding that he didn't want to "do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table".
Trump blocked numerous sanctions on Russia on Friday night, two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky deepened.
Zelensky told NBC News on Sunday that siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin would be a "historic mistake".

Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev has responded to Trump's order by calling it "an important and truly historic moment". He said the sanctions, which were passed by the US Congress and signed into law by the US president in September, would have inflicted "serious damage" on the US and global market.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has described the suspension of the sanctions as a 60-day pause during which their potential impact on the US and global economies would be analysed.
In his Truth Social post, Trump also said Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did", adding "he could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now".
Zelensky has pushed for an end to fighting, and has repeatedly said that Putin doesn't want peace, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel last week.

Despite the international sanctions, Russia has still been able to export oil, much of it to China and India - often at attractive discounts. According to the think-tank Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), China has taken about half of Russia's crude exports, with India accounting for about 37%.

In remarks to a European Union summit, after Trump announced the deal to buy diesel from Russia and said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Putin, Zelensky said it was nice to be among "real leaders".
Ukraine's President Zelensky attended an EU leaders' summit in Brussels on Friday

Zelensky has repeatedly pushed for stringent sanctions to limit funding that Russia can use in its war effort. After the latest move from the US, however, he said he believed the Trump administration would lift more sanctions against Russia.
Ukraine and its European allies criticised Trump's plans to import Russian diesel to help lower US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war.
The deal, according to Zelensky, was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort.

Concerns that Trump is siding with Russia have been heightened by disruption to Starlink, a US-provided satellite system used by Ukraine. That hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from Russian attacks.
Zelensky said US officials had linked speed restrictions to technical issues.
However, he said Ukraine had tested Starlink on EU territory and found it was operating at higher speeds.
Trump has denied both deliberately slowing down the network and a further accusation from Zelensky that the US had stopped sharing defence intelligence.
Trump waives several Russia sanctions as row with Zelensky intensifies
Zelensky says Ukraine has right to defend itself after Trump calls latest strikes a 'disgrace'
Russia accuses Ukraine of attacking oil refinery after Zelensky says strikes to resume

articles.title: Bangladesh says it was not informed of its citizens' execution by Saudi Arabia
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia said it executed two Bangladeshis last week for committing an "indecent act" in a mosque.
body: Two Bangladeshi nationals were executed over an "indecent act" in a mosque, Saudi authorities say
Bangladeshi authorities say they were not informed of the recent execution of two Bangladeshi nationals in the holy city of Mecca until after it had taken place, local media reports.

A Bangladeshi man and woman were executed last Wednesday after being convicted of committing an "indecent act" inside a mosque, according to the Saudi interior ministry. The ministry did not specify the nature of the offending act.
Bangladesh says it has reached out to the Saudi Arabian government to ask for more details about the case.
The two Muslim countries share a close relationship due to their religious affinity and strong economic ties.
More than three million Bangladeshis work and live in Saudi Arabia, mostly in low-paying jobs, and news of the double execution has raised public concern in Bangladesh.

According to the Saudi interior ministry, the two Bangladeshi nationals were convicted and sentenced to death under "tazir", which in Islamic law refers to punishments left to the discretion of the judge.
The ministry statement said they were handed the sentences because of the severity of the offence, and the fact that they violated the "sanctity" of the mosque.
Bangladesh has reached out to the Saudi government about the offences involved and legal proceedings in the case, said state minister for foreign affairs Shama Obaed Islam.
The government would consider next steps, such as the repatriation of the bodies, after getting information from Saudi authorities, Islam said.
She added that the government was committed to safeguarding the welfare and interests of Bangladeshis abroad.

The two executed Bangladeshis were included in a list of prisoners that Saudi Arabia had shared with Bangladesh, upon a request from the Bangladesh Consulate General in Jeddah - but that list did not indicate that the pair had been sentenced to death, the Daily Star reported.
This is not the first time that foreign nationals have been executed by Saudi authorities.
According to Amnesty International, the country has executed around 100 people this year, many of whom are foreigners convicted of drug offences.
In 2011, eight Bangladeshi men were publicly executed in the Saudi Arabian capital of Riyadh after they were found guilty of killing an Egyptian.

Earlier this month, Saudi Arabia overturned a death sentence handed to a Sri Lankan man over a comment he had made on Facebook, which had led to him being convicted of blasphemy. That decision came after the case sparked public outcry in Sri Lanka and spurred diplomatic efforts to seek clemency for the man.

articles.title: Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff survives shooting in Mumbai
articles.summary: Video published by several news outlets shows gunmen firing multiple shots at a car while it is moving past a crowd.
body: Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff did not sustain gunshot wounds in the shooting, police say
Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff has survived a shooting in Mumbai and has not sustained any gunshot wounds, according to Indian police who are investigating the incident.
The 36-year-old was shot at on Sunday evening, while he was in a car that was leaving a football club in the suburb of Juhu.
Several news outlets have published a video showing at least two gunmen firing multiple shots at close range at the front passenger seat of a car while it is slowly moving past a crowd.
The incident has heightened concern about the safety of public figures in India, with some killed or injured in targeted attacks in recent years.
"These attempts to intimidate people will not be tolerated, and we will put an end to this hooliganism," said Eknath Shinde, deputy chief minister of Maharashtra state, where Mumbai is located.
He paid a visit to Shroff after the shooting on Sunday evening, and said the actor and his mother had been left "shaken" by the attack.
Police said two people were injured in the shooting, including Shroff's driver, local media reported.
This is the latest in a string of attacks on some of the country's biggest public figures in recent years.
In 2024, police in India arrested two members of a criminal gang for a gun attack targeting the home of Bollywood actor Salman Khan.
That same year, influential Indian politician Baba Siddique was shot dead in Mumbai.
The son of two actors, Tiger Shroff made his acting debut in 2014 with the romance film Heropanti and went on to star in several films.
He is also a football enthusiast who plays for the professional football club Mumbay FC.

articles.title: Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia
articles.summary: Two men tell of the work they say they have been doing to support Ukrainian intelligence during the war.
body: Watch: Russian saboteur working for Ukraine shares reconnaissance videos

Two Russian men secretly working for Ukraine's intelligence services have given rare accounts of operations they claim to have been involved with, that have targeted military assets and personnel inside Russia.
One of the men, whom we are calling Ivan, claims to have played a role from Russia in Ukrainian drone attacks on strategic bombers and munitions factories on his home soil.
He features in a BBC World Service documentary about the shadowy world of Russian saboteurs.
The documentary, by independent Polish journalist Marcin Mamon, also features a man we are calling Foma, a Russian living in exile in Poland.

Foma runs a network of undercover volunteers in Russia, that surveils high-level officers that the GUR - Ukraine's military intelligence service - is considering targeting, he says. He stresses they are never involved in the attacks themselves.

He was also tight-lipped about who they were surveilling, but after Lt Gen Fanil Sarvarov was assassinated in December last year in Moscow, Foma admitted he had provided the Ukrainians with intelligence on him.
Lt Gen Fanil Sarvarov was killed in Moscow last year by an explosive device hidden under his car
There have been previous media reports of Russian sabotage groups, but it is rare to get access to someone operating on the ground, like Ivan, explaining alleged activities.

The GUR has confirmed that Ivan and Foma are both working for the agency. But it also has acknowledged that it cannot know the full picture. When Ivan's handler was pressed on whether he could be trusted, the handler replied: "I'm not sure of anyone, except myself."
And both the GUR and the men are cautious about how much detail they share, making it impossible to verify the activities the men claim to have carried out.

The broad tactics Ivan and Foma describe, however, have been acknowledged by the Ukrainian authorities. Kyiv has spoken of its strategy of co-ordinated drone attacks on what it claims are legitimate targets inside Russia, and has acknowledged it uses secret agents for this.

There have also been several political assassinations in Russia since the start of the war. As a matter of policy, Ukraine never officially admits or claims responsibility for targeted attacks, though a Ukrainian intelligence officer has previously admitted to the BBC it was behind the killing of senior military figure Lt Gen Igor Kirillov in December 2024.
It is difficult to confirm how many Russians are doing this kind of work for Ukraine. According to Foma, they number about 300-500, though this is impossible to verify.
Shadowmen: Russians working with Ukraine
Two men tell of secret operations inside Russia.
If you are outside the UK, watch on YouTube, external and listen to the BBC World Service Documentary Podcast - Shadowmen: Russians working with Ukraine
Ivan and Foma say they are both opposed not just to Russia's war in Ukraine, but to President Vladimir Putin's regime - and believe his political future depends on the war's outcome.
"At the moment... I think the [Putin] regime might fall if they lose the war… Through our actions... we are trying to speed this up," Ivan says.
His work, he told Mamon, involved surveilling military sites, and locating places to hide drone components, in preparation for potential attacks on Russian assets.
"When these [drone] components are combined… it turns out a formidable weapon, which with a single blow can destroy an object that costs many, many millions of dollars," Ivan said.
He sent Mamon a video which showed him apparently hiding explosives near a Russian military airfield.
If he had been caught, he would have been charged with terrorism, and jailed for decades.

Foma's work is different - he operates remotely, training his volunteers in Russia, online. Mamon watched him conducting one such tutorial - on how to trail a senior military official marked for surveillance.
Foma explained how he taught his undercover volunteers to trail Russian officers

"You will get a file... from me or a colleague… with the proposed target. The file will contain [the target's] photo, his data, his details, date of birth, age, and a description of him. There'll be information on his car, if he has one. When you go to the target, don't take a phone," he told his volunteers.
Foma was once part of the Russian elite, so he claims to have a unique set of contacts and constant flow of insider information.
He showed Mamon on his laptop how he mapped military targets.
"This shows a database... the location of storage warehouses, and military units. Where generals live… Where the pilots of strategic bombers who shell Ukraine live.
"In order to break the system, you need to understand how it works. Then you can aim for their weak points."

He said there were about "three dozen" people in his network split between Russia, Ukraine and elsewhere in Europe, with the contingent outside Russia providing logistical support, such as tracking targets' digital footprints.
Foma stressed that the GUR suggests the targets to be surveilled, but that he and his team check for themselves that these individuals should be considered military criminals.
"As a rule… we also check the data [on that person]… Only after that we say whether we work or not."
But he argued that his team's actions were justified.
"I want people who do terrible things on behalf of Putin and Russia in Ukraine… to understand that they'll have to pay for it. I want them to get scared."
Foma stressed that he only passed on intelligence to the Ukrainians, and his network did not carry out any assassinations themselves.

Of the assassination of Gen Sarvarov, killed in December 2025, he later texted Mamon to say: "Keeping track of him took quite an effort. He lived alternately with his mistress and his colleague. Covered his tracks and constantly changed his schedule."
But Foma did not share any plans with Mamon and the BBC in advance.
Ivan, however, was tight-lipped about the work he had been involved with, even after the event.
Foma did his own digging on Ivan.

After checking with his military intelligence contacts in both Ukraine and Russia, he thought it likely that Ivan had been involved in a plan to strike Russia's largest military drone factory at Yelabuga in June last year, external. One person was reported to have been killed in the incident.
Ivan stressed that the aim is always to try to avoid harming civilians.
Operations have clearly been risky for Ivan too.
"The most serious case was when my car was stopped for inspection and I had the handmade explosives on me. The risk was very high - however as you can see, I was not detected," he said.
To mitigate the risk of being compromised, "there is no clear structure" to the work, he said, adding he had never met and did not know the identity of others he had been working alongside.
Foma has the same rule for his operatives.
"As soon as you start gathering people in groups, in general chats… leaving a mark on the internet, with a high probability this whole group will be quickly detained or destroyed," he said.
Ivan stressed there were few people left in Russia suitable for this kind of work.
"Most of the ideological people have either left the country or are already behind bars," he said.

Many Russians involved in sabotage work on their native soil are therefore either oblivious - for example lorry drivers unaware that their cargoes have been compromised - or are individuals who have been paid, the BBC understands.

Ivan, on the other hand, says he is doing this work for ideological reasons - he used to be a member of the political opposition. As such, his movements would be expected to be monitored closely by the Russian authorities.
So it was a surprise that he managed to frequently leave Russia and return.
Marcin waiting to meet Ivan in Georgia - we were surprised by Ivan's apparent freedom to travel
Mamon persuaded Ivan to drive him into the Georgian desert, where they could speak freely - and asked him how the Ukrainians could trust him.
"You go to a third country… where [Ukraine's] agents meet you… and conduct lie detector tests," Ivan told him.

Mamon asked Ivan to put him in touch with one of his GUR handlers in Ukraine. This man immediately rang Ivan on speaker phone - apparently demonstrating that Ivan worked for him. They spoke in code, referring to "repairs at the school".
But later, the handler admitted he could not rule out the possibility Ivan might work for the Russians too, either voluntarily or under duress.
Foma thinks the fact that Ivan can travel freely does not necessarily constitute a red flag.

"There are all sorts of holes in [the country's governance], and if you know them, or are just lucky, then you can jump through the holes… and live in the system. Like a mouse in a piece of cheese," he told Mamon.

Perhaps more compellingly, if Ivan had also been spying for FSB, it would seem likely that he would share what he knew of Ukraine's attack plans with the Russian agency. More than a year before a devastating strike by more than 100 Ukrainian drones, Ivan had been telling Marcin there would be a major attack on strategic bombers on military airfields across Russia, though he never said when or where.

articles.title: Warning signs over threats to Australian politicians were rising before MP hit by car
articles.summary: The apparent attack on MP Helen Haines suggests the worst fears of politicians and public figures appear to have been realised.
body: Police have been guarding the hospital in Melbourne where independent MP Helen Haines is being treated

As increasingly frequent acts of violence against politicians have shocked the globe in recent years, Australia has watched on with a contradictory feeling: that attacks like that could not happen here, and that it was only a matter of time until they did.

Australians will tell you this is a largely peaceful society with a comparatively civil public discourse. Violence targeting politicians has been rare, the bungled assassination of Labor leader Arthur Calwell in 1966 now a distant and fleeting memory.
But MPs and public figures – backed by experts – have been warning of a volcano of threats against them as social cohesion cracks, polarisation intensifies and the tone of debate grows hotter.
And on Monday, their worst fears appear to have been realised.
Independent MP Helen Haines was struck by a car and severely injured outside her office in the regional Victorian town of Wangaratta.
Police say a 43-year-old man was arrested at the scene, and a knife seized, but they have not said Haines was hit deliberately.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, however, swiftly described the incident as an apparent attack.

He was briefed by federal police – whose counter terror squad is helping state officers investigate – and told the national broadcaster: "This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear."
Though he stressed no motive had been confirmed, Albanese earlier got emotional as he talked about the growing fear amongst MPs that they would end up targets.
Australian MP critically injured after being hit by car in apparent attack
What we know about apparent attack on Australian MP hit by car

Earlier this year Albanese himself was evacuated from his official residence over a bomb threat. As of August, about 20 cases in which people were accused of making violent threats against him were winding their way through courts around the country.

In recent years, politicians here have been mailed bullets. Female MPs – and in some cases their children – have been threatened with sexual violence. A Jewish MP's office has been firebombed, a Sydney mayor's car has been torched and countless other politicians have had their workplaces vandalised.

Just last week Small Business Minister Anne Aly said she had received a wave of death threats after a politician from the opposition said she should be "shamed and stoned in the square" over a tax policy.
According to government statistics, there were 1,067 reports of "harassing and threatening behaviour" against "high office holders" in the year to June: an increase on last year.
"We tend to bury our head in the sand and say, 'Not here', but this has been happening now for well over a decade," Josh Roose, a Deakin University Professor on violent extremism, tells the BBC.

Socioeconomic strain, growing mental health problems in the community, "grifters" who benefit politically or financially from whipping up further discontent, and a "carcinogenic" online environment are drivers of the trend, he says, which has dramatically escalated since the pandemic.
But the political class must also take responsibility for their role, he adds.

"We've seen a willingness to cross previously sacred terrain - you know, not targeting individuals, not targeting their families - but we now see that this is part and parcel of Australian political life.
"This is occurring at both ends of the political spectrum."
And experts like him warn it is not just politicians who are vulnerable: it is members of the media, academics, court officials and other public figures too.
Helen Haines at Parliament House in Canberra
Mike Burgess, the head of Australia's spy agency, has warned for years that the spectre of political violence is looming in Australia.

"Just as climate change increases the likelihood of extreme weather but does not forecast specific storms, politically motivated violence, including acts of terrorism, is more likely even though we cannot predict a specific attack," he said in his annual threat assessment for 2026.
And the Federal Police have said it is not just ideology motivating cases in recent times. "Grievance" is radicalising people.
"They're feeling distanced, they're feeling alone, they're looking for something to attach to, to give them meaning and purpose," Commissioner Krissy Barrett told the ABC earlier this month.

There have been frustrated rumblings in Canberra from some MPs who say security arrangements have not changed with the climate and – if a political motivation for this incident is confirmed – one of the greatest tenets of the nation's political culture could now be at risk.
It is not abnormal for you to run into your local member at the shops, or chat to them at the footy, and many open up their offices for constituents who want to raise concerns or share ideas.
Haines is particularly renowned and respected for that, Albanese said on Monday night.
"Here in Australia, it is a good thing that politicians are able to go about their community and engage with people," he said.

"I don't want to see a political system in which you can't have conversations with people at the supermarket, in the street, at street meetings, public forums – that's an important part of our democracy."

articles.title: In pictures: French landmarks damaged and destroyed by violent protesters
articles.summary: France is used to protests but the violence and damage seen across the country is shocking many people.
body: Local curfews may come into force in French towns following a weekend of disorder.
Most of the protesters were peaceful in expressing their opposition to rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.
But others - dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas - set fire to cars, shops and buildings.
The scale of the destruction - including to some iconic landmarks - has shocked many in a country used to street protests.
The damage in the capital city is extensive. Shop fronts have been broken and stores looted.
Kiosks, vehicles and buildings were set alight and destroyed close to some of the city's most recognisable areas, including here at Place De La Republique in Paris
Front doors and windows were broken down as looting broken out in several cities
Some groups erected barricades on the Champs-Elysees in Paris
The iconic Place de la Republique was vandalised, too.
A yellow vest - representative of the movement which helped co-ordinate the weekend protests - was draped around the body of the Statue of the Republic, erected in 1883.
Groups of rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, took over parts of the capital and wreaked havoc.
Tear gas and stun grenades were fired at hundreds of people but police struggled to contain smaller groups of people roving around the city attack businesses.
The full extent of the damage did not become clear until dawn broke on Sunday.
This bakery was one of several businesses set on fire in Paris
Some groups piled rental bikes in the middle of roads and set them alight
Cars were set alight close to the Porte Saint-Denis in the capital
Further south in Marseille, protesters broke into the city hall by using a metal fence as a battering ram.
A bust of Marianne - symbol of the French Republic - was damaged and knocked to the floor in Marseille as people ransacked the building.
City Mayor Benoît Payan was furious with the "almost total lack of control" by the security forces.
"The world's sixth largest power does not deserve this. The world is watching us, this morning we are the shame of Europe," he said.
In the city of Lyon, Mayor Grégory Doucet said the burning of the city's tourist office, housed in a 19th Century building, was "a tragedy".
Chaos around the tourist office in Lyon as flames engulf it
Fire crews also battled a fire at Limoges town hall, which caused part of the building to collapse. Local officials said the town hall was "largely lost".
"A wild horde" had "deliberately" set fire to the 143-year-old building, said Maurice Barate, the prefect for the Haute-Vienne department.
In Limoges, the spire at the top of the ornate city hall has been destroyed by the fire
French authorities have admitted they lost control of cities to the protesters.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez offered his resignation - which has been rejected.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has given local mayors the power to introduce partial curfews in some parts of the country, which he says is designed to protect people and businesses.
But the French are holding their breath - in anticipation of another chapter in this protest next Saturday.
Are student protests being manipulated ahead of France's presidential election?

French PM calls for cities to impose curfews after violent weekend protests

articles.title: Funding shortages force World Food Programme to cut aid to Gaza
articles.summary: The number of people helped by the UN agency in the Palestinian territory will drop by about a third - from 1.6 million to 1.1 million.
body: Dalal al-Dahdouh said the WFP food handouts her family received were insufficient even before the cuts

One of the main suppliers of food aid to the Gaza Strip, the World Food Programme (WFP), says that it is being forced to "drastically reduce lifesaving assistance" to the Palestinian territory due to funding shortages.
Overall, the number of people helped by the UN agency will drop by about a third - from 1.6 million to 1.1 million.
The cuts will hit as winter approaches and at a time when many families in Gaza are still struggling to feed themselves.
One effect is that the number of hot meals that are currently being provided by community kitchens will be cut from 250,000 to 150,000 each day.
Families living in hard-to-reach areas, for example near the so-called Yellow Line, which demarcates Israel's area of military control, will receive a meal every other day instead of daily.
Nearly all of Gaza's 2.1 million population remains displaced and two-thirds rely on food aid to survive.
Mervat al-Satari, a mother-of-five, says the cuts are a "disaster"

"It's a disaster! What will we do with these reduced rations? How will we provide for the little ones?" said Mervat al-Satari, a displaced Palestinian mother-of-five at a camp in the al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis after being told of the WFP's news. "Sometimes we wait for these meals to eat."

"This will affect us a lot. The daily aid was somehow ticking the box but now it will be every two days," said Sawsan Bahloul, who is also from al-Mawasi and is a mother of three. She added that the portions given by the community kitchen - usually pasta or lentils with occasional potatoes and aubergines - were already too small to feed her family.
The Palestine director for the WFP, Shaun Hughes, is clear that the cuts are being made because of finances, and "not because the needs are coming down, or because we don't have access - we do."
Nearly all of Gaza's 2.1 million people are displaced, with many living in camps like those in al-Mawasi

Already, since July, there have been reductions in cash transfers provided to some half a million people, meaning they have less money to buy food in local markets. The number of Gazans given bags of flour and ration boxes by the WFP will now fall from 1.1 million to 600,000 each month.

The WFP received less than half as much funding for its Palestinian operations in 2026 as in previous years. The agency says it urgently needs $450m (£338m) to maintain "critical" operations over the next six months.
Despite a ceasefire between Hamas and Israel that was agreed a year ago, violence has continued, including almost daily Israeli strikes, and humanitarian conditions in Gaza remain dire.

There has been no reconstruction and little recovery, with Israel tightly controlling the entry of goods through crossings. While food markets are now well stocked, few can afford to buy from them. More than 80% of people in Gaza are unemployed so most of the population relies on aid.
Two-thirds of the population relies on food aid to survive, according to UN-backed experts
Families currently receiving the WFP food handouts complained to the BBC that already these were insufficient and gave them little diversity in their diets.

"The flour isn't enough and the food boxes aren't enough either," said Dalal al-Dahdouh, who is living in the ruins of her home in Gaza City with her family of eight. She fears the new cuts will have "a major impact".

The mother draws a contrast between the current desperate situation and life before the war. "In the past, thank God, we had our own home and a wonderful life. We had fresh vegetables, proper sanitation facilities and our own land," she said. "Now we live entirely on aid, including WFP vouchers."

There is no cooking gas available in Gaza because the Israeli government considers it a "dual use" item that could be used by Hamas for military purposes. Wood is expensive, so many families send their children into the street to find plastic and cardboard to burn as fuel to make bread or heat food.

"It's still a very concerning humanitarian situation, people living in brutal conditions, most people still without a proper home, living in tents, poor access to water and sanitation and healthcare," Hughes of the WFP told the BBC. "Cuts to food assistance are going to compound that hardship that families have been facing for three years now."
Families, including Sawsan Bahloul's, are forced to burn plastic and cardboard as fuel for cooking
Humanitarian workers say that despite a modest improvement in Gaza compared to a year ago, acute food insecurity and the risk of famine returning continue to loom over the territory.

In July, the Integrated Phase Classification (IPC) - the world's foremost experts on food security - reported that two-thirds of the population - 1.4 million people - were "expected to face crisis or worse levels of acute food insecurity in July-December 2026".

For now, the WFP says it can continue supporting bakeries that provide one-third of Gaza's bread needs and provide nutritional assistance to about 300,000 women and children. It also delivers health food snacks to some 200,000 children.
In the occupied West Bank, the WFP is continuing to give assistance to some 200,000 Palestinians, having halved the number of recipients in September.
The agency says food insecurity is rising in the territory mostly due to increased Israeli settler violence and Palestinian displacement.

Reports of violence against women in Gaza surge, UN agency finds

articles.title: A wave of homemade, synthetic drugs sweeps US and deepens crisis
articles.summary: BBC News hears from users, dealers, prison and recovery workers as the country battles with a deadly new drug epidemic.
body: The BBC’s Quentin Sommerville joins officers at Cook County as they carry out an early morning raid
Warning: This story contains descriptions of drug-taking from the start and discusses suicide

The few grains of fentanyl sit in the silver foil as a straw, held between Mike's lips, hovers above, with a cigarette lighter below. The 48-year-old army veteran is crouched low in an alleyway in Columbus, Ohio's Linden neighbourhood.
"This drug will damn near make you do anything, unfortunately," he says.
The hit he's smoking cost three or four dollars.
"You can snort too much and you can't take it back. Kind of like a gunshot. Can't call the bullet back," he says.
He burns the foil and inhales. As the opioid takes hold, he grips the fence behind him. He sways as a low moan comes from deep in his throat - he could be humming a tune.

We've spent a few days with Mike - he's been our guide through the neighbourhood's back streets. Everyone seems to know him and he's regarded fondly. He helps out at a local pawn shop and gas station, and that's how he feeds his 20-year-old opioid addiction.
Synthetic opioids are more powerful and in plentiful supply, and they have transformed the drugs landscape.

Fentanyl, which is entirely man-made, is 50 to 100 times more powerful than heroin, which is cultivated from poppies. It is now often cut with synthetic tranquillisers, which make reviving overdose victims more difficult. These are homemade threats, where cocktails of synthetics can be made in American basements and bathtubs.
America's War on Drugs: The Synthetic Wave
Extraordinary access shows how strong synthetic drugs are changing America's drug crisis.
"This drug will damn near make you do anything, unfortunately," says Mike as he lights up a few grains of fentanyl
Mike, a former army veteran, acts as our guide through the neighbourhood's back streets

We have Naloxone (brand name Narcan) in our pockets, in case anyone on our team comes into contact with fentanyl or anyone around us overdoses. It's a nasal spray that immediately reverses opioid overdoses and its widespread adoption has transformed the number of fatal overdoses in the United States.

At its peak in 2022, 110,000 Americans were dying from overdoses, mostly from opioids. The number has been dropping since, down to around 70,000 last year. But that doesn't mean the opioid crisis is over.
It's likely that the reversal drug in my pocket, which has saved tens of thousands of drug users' lives, would not have worked on Mike. Because he wasn't just smoking fentanyl.

The pupils in his milky blue eyes shrink to pin pricks. "Opioids make your pupils go smaller, but not that small," he says in a singsong voice. Even the fentanyl, dangerous enough on its own, has other synthetics added.
When we ask what he thinks his drugs have been cut with, he replies: "Xylazine, and the one we can't pronounce."
Medetomidine is what he means. Like xyalzine, it is also referred to as tranq and both are synthetic animal tranquilisers. "Large animal tranquilisers," as one recovery expert told me.

They help prolong the high from the fentanyl but are a sedative that slows breathing and, importantly, naloxone doesn't work against them. Xylazine also causes necrotic skin ulcers, wounds so deep they can make it down to the bone and are difficult to treat.

At the Glenwood Church on the other side of town, members of the Hope Dealer Community, a recovery group, gather for a weekly meeting. For many, their struggles are written in their care-worn faces, and their eyes are those of survivors of a great trauma.
They take to the stage at the front of the church and share their stories with a brutal and courageous honesty.

One man tells the story of his overdose in July 2022. Two paramedics worked on him, trying to save his life. He had naloxone drips in both arms. They hit him with the opioid reversal three times to no avail. "That's it, I'm gonna call it," said one of the medics. But the other insisted on one more try, and it was that which saved his life.

As the crowd shouts encouragement, Tonya takes to the lectern. She recounts how her nephew died of an overdose while she was overdosing at the same time from crack cocaine, a stimulant spiked with fentanyl, a synthetic opioid.
"It's not luck. I'm supposed to be here," she says with tears in her eyes. The audience yells its agreement.
Members of the Hope Dealer Community, a recovery group, gather for a weekly meeting at Glenwood Church
One of those gathered at the church, Tonya, recounts how her nephew died of an overdose while she was overdosing at the same time
Both in Columbus, and later in Chicago, we would hear of crack cocaine users who had died of overdoses after their drugs contained fentanyl. On the street, it's called a "hot dose".
"In the last 12 months in Franklin County [Columbus], 78% of fatal overdoses are from stimulants," explains Scott Sanders, 65, who runs Hope Dealers.
Scott is almost 10 years sober, a powerfully built man in his early 60s with an electric energy. When he asks the room to raise their hands if anyone has overdosed, most of the gathering does so.

"The crisis has just shifted," Scott tells me afterwards. "The tragedy is stimulant users who are purchasing crack think that's what they're getting, and they're not. They're getting crack mixed with fentanyl or other opioid cocktails and overdosing without being aware of it."
Scott Sanders, 65, is almost 10 years sober and runs Hope Dealers
Overdose deaths among black men in Ohio are actually increasing, he adds.

His organisation works with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) on a drug sampling programme. Participants bring their needles or pipes for swabbing and the samples are sent to the CDC's laboratory in North Carolina.
That's how we learned that Mike's instincts were right, he likely wasn't just smoking fentanyl. One of the drug kits he brought in tested positive for medetomidine.

"The drug supply in 2026 is this: we think we are buying crack but we're not, we're buying a number of different things," says Scott. "Today it is mixed, not just cut, but mixed with other drugs such as fentanyl or meth, and then other adulterants chemicals that are made in basements."
And it was basement-made synthetic drugs that would cause a dramatic increase in overdose deaths one state over, in Illinois.
Watch the documentary on YouTube, external
I meet a dealer in Chicago who works for the Mexican cartels selling fentanyl. He would only speak to us if we agreed to mask his identity.
Challenged on his role in the 50,000 people dying each year because of the opioid crisis, he says he knows it is wrong. But when asked why he keeps doing it, he said the end justifies the means.

He told me that despite the latest efforts by the US government to target the cartels by declaring them terrorist groups and labelling fentanyl a weapon of mass destruction, his supply chain is as strong as ever.
When I ask him if the targeting of boats containing suspected traffickers by the Trump administration has made any difference, he replies that his product is still getting through from Mexico.
"If it doesn't go over the wall, it goes under the wall. If it doesn't go through the border, it comes through the top border. This game is about adaptability."
And when I asked what has changed in his business, his answer was clear.
"Synthetics. We haven't seen... what synthetics can do yet. It's not even the tip of the iceberg," he tells me.

Chicago's largest jail, one of the largest jails in America, is Cook County. Traditional drugs were usually brought into the jail in body cavities, so the jail had the same body scanners you find at airports to prevent that happening.

"In 2023, all of a sudden we saw a spike in overdose deaths, but then hand in hand with that we saw, around persons that had either passed away or people we revived, paper all over the place," explains Sheriff Tom Dart, who runs the jail. "We were seeing paper that was being burned and all of this was completely novel."
The facility, which averages one or two overdose deaths a year, lost eight inmates that year to fatal seizures.
Security footage shows prisoners spasming and collapsing. It also showed them lighting paper in microwaves in the cell block kitchens.
It was indeed, as Dart said, a novel approach. Drugs were being mailed into the jail soaked in the pages of books and in letters.
"Cannabinoids and being soaked in a range of other things that were then subsequently lit on fire and inhaled to get high", the sheriff explained.
Cannabinoids, sometimes know as K2, are an entirely synthetic version of a cannabis plant extract. They are extremely dangerous and were to blame for the fatal seizures.
In Chicago's largest jail, drugs were soaked in the pages of books and in letters

In August, I joined Dart's corrections officers as they prepared for an early morning raid on the jail's high security D block. Around two dozen officers tread lightly and speak in hushed tones as they gather outside the block door. "Don't let them hear you. Silence, silence," commands one of the officers leading the search.
As the officers rush in, I smell burning paper in the air and can hear the sound of toilets flushing, presumably as contraband is hurriedly disposed of.
As the search gets under way, the focus is on any paper in the cells - the books and letters belonging to inmates.

The detainees are escorted to a holding area as the cells are turned over. Every scrap of paper in the rooms is checked by the officers. There are burn marks on the vents in many of the cells, where inmates place smoulder tapers that allow them to ignite the drug-soaked paper.
Now every piece of post that enters the jail is scanned for moisture. Somewhere between a quarter and a fifth of all packages and letters test positive and are rejected.
Between a quarter and a fifth of all packages and letters that enter the jail test positive for moisture

articles.title: Houthi attack kills 53 in biggest single loss of life since Yemen civil war reignited
articles.summary: More than 200 mostly young people said to be injured after ballistic missile attack on training camp for government forces
body: At least 53 people have been killed in a Houthi ballistic missile attack on a training camp for Yemeni government security forces, making it the largest single loss of life since the country’s civil war reignited in September.

The attack on al-Alam camp in the southern Shabwa province was said to have injured more than 200 others, mostly young recruits, and was described as a disaster by the country’s UN-recognised government. The injured were taken from the police and army training camp in the Jardan district to a hospital in the local capital, Ataq, where pleas for blood donations were made.
Related: Yemen civil war: what sparked latest escalation and who is involved?

There will be an inquiry into how so many troops were left so exposed to a Houthi attack. In mid-September, the group began a fresh push on forces backing the UN-recognised government by pushing south along the Red Sea coast to try to take control of the Bab al-Mandab waterway.

Reliable assessments of the death toll in the fighting over the last month are hard to gather, but it is running into the many thousands. A Saudi airstrike on Sunday killed nine, including five children and two women.

Rashad al-Alimi, the president of the UN-recognised government, said those killed on Monday were new recruits, and he vowed an immediate hard response. He said the incident “affirmed that targeting the recruits reflects the Houthi militias’ approach of resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they face pressures or their Iranian-backed sabotage plots falter”.
On Monday he phoned the UN secretary general, António Guterres, to ask for the UN to classify the Houthis as a foreign terrorist organisation.

The Shabwa provincial authority said: “Targeting recruits constitutes a military escalation and a blatant assault on the province’s security.” Its governor, Awad bin al-Wazir, visited the wounded in hospitals, and called for extra air defences, saying troops were fighting across six fronts.

The killings underline the dangers of large numbers of troops gathering in one place within reach of the Houthi ballistic missile arsenal. The training camp was struck by three ballistic missiles while the recruits lined up in formation.
Houthi forces have also cut the road between government-run Shabwa and the Houthi-run Bayda governorate.

The Houthi military spokesperson said: “Our armed forces targeted the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations in al-Alam camp, which is run by Saudi officers in the eastern regions. The targeting resulted in the fall of dozens of dead and wounded from the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations, including Saudi officers.

“We warn the deceived ones against responding to the Saudi enemy’s calls to lure them with his defiled money to the pyres of death, and to exploit them instead of his soldiers who are indifferent to their lives.”

A Yemen government spokesperson said the site struck was not a military target linked to the current fighting but “a training centre where new recruits in the internal security forces of Shabwa governorate receive training and qualification programmes.”
They added: “This reveals the criminal nature of this assault, which targeted young people in the preparation and qualification phase to carry out their security duties, far from the frontlines.”

Separately the Houthis claim to have hit the anti-Houthi Giant Brigades of southern Yemen in six strikes in the areas of al-Suqya and Ras al-Ara. Southern forces are said to have been making progress in edging Houthi forces out of control of the area around the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrowest waterway taking ships from the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.

Fighting is also under way as Houthis try to mount a siege of Taiz, where citizens have been calling for greater air protection. In the city there seems to be a determination not to capitulate, but conditions are deteriorating as Houthis close access points.
It is not clear whether the Houthis have decided to slow the pace of attacks on Saudi airports and energy installations, or they are running low on munitions.
The Saudi Aramco headquarters was struck last weekend and some airlines have said they will not yet resume using Riyadh airport. The airport reopened at the weekend after being attacked this month.

Egypt’s parliament has postponed a vote on whether to send troops to Saudi Arabia despite extending the debate to a second day as MPs demanded more than two minutes each to speak. The vote is now likely to be held next week.

A two-thirds majority is required, and some opposition parties have signalled their intention to vote against or abstain. Disputes centre on the extent of the mission and whether it will involve sending troops into Yemen to help Saudi Arabia, and whether Egyptian troops inside Saudi Arabia would become targets for Houthi attacks.
The delay also gives the Egyptians time to see if Iran can persuade the Houthis to hold back, and for Saudi Arabia to confirm the renewal of badly needed loans to Egypt.

Egypt has resisted any ground intervention in Yemen, dating back to the 1962-67 war, when Gamal Abdel Nasser sent troops to back the republicans in North Yemen against the Saudi- and British-backed royalists. The incursion was intended to be minimal, but escalated to as many as 70,000 soldiers. Estimates of Egyptians killed range from 10,000-26,000.

articles.title: Why are people protesting across Europe?
articles.summary: School conditions, unaffordable housing and the cost of living have brought demonstrators on to the streets in several countries
body: Young people have been taking to the streets across Europe, including in Spain, France and Portugal, to protest over their unhappiness at the state of schools and the wider cost of living crisis.

In France, high school pupils have clashed with police in often violent protests over long hours, missing teachers, dilapidated classrooms and an opaque university admissions system. Pupils routinely miss months of teaching due to unfilled staff absences.

Other demonstrators soon joined in, voicing their unhappiness about rising living costs, including over fuel prices after US bombing in effect caused the closure of the strait of Hormuz. The General Confederation of Labour, one of France’s largest unions, has backed the protests and called for lower prices, higher pensions and boosted wages.
The French president, Emmanuel Macron, is nearing the end of his time in the Élysée Palace after serving two terms.
Over the Pyrenees in Spain, activists took to the streets in September over housing prices.

The protests were triggered by the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home after an investment fund hiked her rent by 230%. Maricarmen Abascal died a fortnight later after being admitted to hospital.
Protesters have called for rent freezes, halting the evictions of vulnerable people and the regulation of short-term and room rentals.

Similar pleas were made across the Iberian border in Portugal on Saturday, when hundreds gathered in central Lisbon. Portuguese housing prices more than doubled between 2015 and 2024, roughly twice as fast as the EU average, according to official data.

Squeezed household budgets were also at the centre of marches in Milan. Masked rioters seemingly later seized on the protests to throw stones, paving blocks and other objects at riot police and setting fire to barricades made from bar tables. There were also clashes between police and protesters in Turin and Bologna.

Meanwhile, protests in Albania against the prime minister, Edi Rama, entered their seventh day on Monday. Demonstrators have said they are unhappy with perceived corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards.
The education protests in France began in late September, a week after the start of the school year. Protests soon also began springing up in Portugal and Belgium.

In France, demonstrations reached a high point on Saturday as about half a million people turned out to protest against the surging cost of living and join the students demanding better conditions at their schools. That day there were also marches in Belgium, Portugal and Italy.
In Albania, protests have been taking place since the summer, triggered by a luxury coastal development backed by Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.

In France, the government has said it will deploy 3,000 more substitute teachers to deal with shortages, and include students in decision-making for schools. It also scrapped plans to increase some university registration fees, which it had announced for next year’s budget.
Fuel protests in mid-September led to an announcement by the Élysée that the government would increase petrol subsidies for certain industries.

Spain’s Socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, attempted to pass emergency housing legislation that included a ban on evictions until 2030 and the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room.

The legislation’s defeat at the hands of rightwing and far-right parties in parliament led Sánchez to call a snap election for 29 November, as he told the public he needed a “broader progressive majority” to get new reforms through.

In recent days, the protests have been eclipsed by the violence that played out on the fringes. On Sunday night Macron said it was “unbearable to see our streets ransacked” while, hours later, France’s prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, called for “very limited” and “localised” curfews.

Macron said a distinction must be drawn between what he described as genuine, peaceful demonstrators who were making demands over the cost of living and the education system, and others who “destroy, ransack and loot”.

His interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, appeared to signal the French government was not willing to concede further, as he blamed “far-left” protesters and “criminals who looted and ransacked” buildings across France. The country will go to the polls in April 2027.
Meanwhile, the protests continue. In Paris, about a dozen demonstrators blocked the entrance to the Louvre on Monday, leaving tourists milling outside the world’s most-visited museum.
In Spain, housing campaigners have vowed to keep up the pressure on politicians to address soaring costs, announcing plans for a general strike on 11 November.

articles.title: Ferocious criticism from all sides underlines Macron’s isolation
articles.summary: French president has compounded impression of arrogance with strategic errors – and consequences could be profound
body: The near-universal chorus of condemnation that greeted Emmanuel Macron’s address to the nation on Sunday, after one of the most violent days of rioting and looting in France’s recent history, was a stark reflection of just how weakened he now is.

Speaking from his office at the Élysée Palace, the president delivered an eight-minute speech expressing “anger and shame” after a weekend in which a town hall was set ablaze, 2,000-plus shops were looted, 2,300 people were arrested and 1,000 police injured.

A month-long protest by high school pupils over crumbling and crowded classrooms converged with broader frustrations over soaring living costs, rapidly widening inequality and falling public spending, bringing together students, teachers, trade unionists and a resurrected gilets jaunes movement.
Related: French prime minister calls for ‘local and partial’ curfews after riots

Those largely peaceful protests were swiftly hijacked by masked groups who torched vehicles, ransacked businesses and severely damaged public infrastructure, including setting fire to Limoges’ city hall and invading that of Marseille.

Macron acknowledged the “deep anxiety” of young people but offered no concrete policy initiatives, no cabinet reshuffle and no new public spending, merely telling his prime minister to organise consultations and asking opposition politicians to take a stand.

The response, across the political spectrum, was damning. The Greens’ leader, Marine Tondelier, said that rather than “even beginning to make any kind of mea culpa”, Macron was “summoning us to the PM’s office like pupils to the blackboard”.

On the far right, the National Rally’s Jordan Bardella called the speech “lamentable” and said Macron had “nothing left to say” to the French. The party’s figurehead, Marine Le Pen, said the country was “caught in a vice between violence and impotence”.

The centre-right’s Bruno Retailleau said Macron was “totally overwhelmed”, while on the radical left, Jean-Luc Mélenchon accused the president of relying on “inaction and police brutality” in doomed hopes that the protests would simply fizzle out.

Perhaps most damagingly, even Macron’s former prime minister Édouard Philippe said he would have preferred “decisions and initiatives that might lead to a return to order and the restoration of state authority … Our country needs to be governed.”

Criticism is to be expected from rivals positioning themselves six months before a presidential election to choose Macron’s successor. But its sheer ferocity underlines his isolation, the disdain in which he is held, and the anger he inspires.

It is a structural trap that he has largely set for himself. Macron came to power in 2017 as a “Jupiterian” president – a deliberate strategy aimed at elevating the head of state above daily politics, projecting distant authority and technocratic brilliance.

But over nine years in the Élysée, that high-handed style – partly born, his critics say, of Macron’s complete lack of basic political experience as an elected official in a town hall or as a constituency MP – has morphed into perceived arrogance and detachment.

It has been compounded by catastrophic strategic errors, and France’s spiralling economic problems. Macron lost a functional parliamentary majority by refusing to meaningfully campaign between the presidential and legislative elections of 2022.

Two years later he dissolved the national assembly. That gamble backfired spectacularly, with voters returning an even more deadlocked parliament split between a divided left, a much-diminished centrist bloc and Le Pen’s far right.

Without a working majority, the government repeatedly resorted to controversial constitutional manoeuvres to force through laws without a parliamentary vote, laying it – and Macron – open to further accusations of democratic illegitimacy.

Compounding that institutional deadlock is a looming fiscal crisis. In decades gone by, French presidents facing mass protests on the streets could in effect buy a degree of social tranquility with targeted spending packages or public sector concessions.

But France’s national debt, at 119% of GDP, is at its highest level since 1946. Its budget deficit, at 5.1%, is also among the highest in the EU. There is just no money in the bank to ease the cost of living squeeze that brought 550,000 people on to the streets on Saturday.

The markets are worried: France’s borrowing costs are higher than Greece’s. And with few fiscal options, the government’s clearest response – in time-honoured French tradition – has been teargas and baton charges, sometimes against schoolchildren, further aggravating tensions.

The consequences for the presidential election could be profound. The centrist coalition built around Macron’s brand has all but collapsed. If the protests and violence persist, the main beneficiary will be the law-and-order champions of the far right.

Jean-Baptiste Moreau, an influential former MP from Macron’s party with whom the largely lame-duck president still occasionally speaks, reportedly went so far this weekend as to suggest he should resign and call early presidential elections.
“Macron still thinks he can change things,” he told Le Monde. “But at the moment, Marine Le Pen is on a direct path to the Élysée Palace.”

articles.title: Jim Churm obituary
articles.summary: Other lives: Nurse and physiotherapist who played his part in the D-day landings as a medic on landing craft
body: My father, Jim Churm, who has died aged 102, was a D-day veteran and former Royal Navy medic; he later enjoyed a long career in nursing and physiotherapy.

Jim joined the navy as an 18-year-old during the second world war and trained as a sick berth attendant before being assigned to landing craft operations. On D-day, 6 June 1944, he sailed from Newhaven in East Sussex as the leading medic aboard a landing craft involved in the assault on Sword Beach, one of the five main landing areas along the Normandy coast during the allied invasion of France.

His primary responsibility was to care for sick and injured personnel, but with crews stretched to their limits, he also helped operate winches and undertook general seamanship duties. He had to be ready to transfer between vessels whenever medical assistance was needed.

Jim made two crossings from Britain to Normandy on landing craft that were particularly vulnerable to enemy mines, lacking the protective equipment fitted to larger naval vessels. Afterwards he spent a short time back in the UK before being posted to Egypt.

After the war he qualified as a nurse, specialising in orthopaedics in Birmingham before undertaking physiotherapy training in Liverpool and then becoming a chartered physiotherapist, first in Leicester and then in Blackburn at the Queen’s Park hospital and Blackburn Royal Infirmary.

Later he took on private work at Our Lady of Compassion hospital in the town and had his own surgeries in Accrington and Blackburn. For a time, in the late 1960s, he was also the physiotherapist for two local football clubs, Blackburn Rovers and Accrington Stanley.

Born in Nottingham, he was the son of Arthur, an oil industry worker, and his wife, Miriam (nee Cooper), who divorced when Jim was young. After attending Claremont school in Nottingham he joined the navy despite having secured an apprenticeship with a butcher, which was a reserved wartime occupation.

In later life Jim was quietly proud of the small part he played in the liberation of France, and was keen to emphasise the often-overlooked role of landing craft crews, without whom the troops could not have reached the beaches. He was a committed supporter of remembrance activities and regularly attended Royal British Legion Scotland events, where his experiences, wisdom and humility were greatly valued.

In retirement he and his wife, Sheila (nee Cahill), who was also a physiotherapist and whom he married in 1952, retired to Crossmichael in Kirkcudbrightshire, where they made their home for more than 30 years. Jim became a much-loved member of the local community and particularly enjoyed fishing on Loch Ken.

His 100th birthday was celebrated with a surprise performance by the Royal Marines Band, Scotland, and in 2025 he was made a chevalier of the Légion d’honneur by the French ambassador at the Usher Hall in Edinburgh, during a concert commemorating the 80th anniversary of VE Day.
His life, however, was defined as much by his devotion to family, and by his kindness and commitment to helping others as by his wartime experiences.
Sheila died in 2018; Jim is survived by their three sons, David, Michael and me, 10 grandchildren and five great-grandchildren.

articles.title: France hit by debt sell-off as violent protests unnerve investors
articles.summary: Difference between French and German borrowing costs widens after public buildings burned and shops looted
body: France has been hit by a fresh wave of selling in its bond and stock markets after violent protests over the weekend led to thousands of arrests and left public buildings burned and hundreds of shops looted across the country.
The chaos has spooked investors as analysts worried that it would undermine Paris’s efforts to cut spending and reduce its debt.

The yield on the government’s 10-year bonds rose by as much as 16 basis points to 4.94% on Monday. Yields rise when prices fall, and the bond market sell-off pushed France’s borrowing costs close to a 24-year high.
This widened the difference between the French and German 10-year borrowing costs – which is a metric for the risk premium attached to French debt – towards its highest level in 14 years.

Analysts at Goldman Sachs said European sovereign risk was back in focus, with fiscal concerns about France raising the question of whether there could be a repeat of the eurozone debt crisis of 15 years ago.

“The risks of disorderly market escalation and real economy contagion look notably lower. But the fundamental fiscal challenges for some countries – especially in France – look harder now than in 2011-15,” the investment bank said.
“The issue of how to deal with fundamental sovereign risk remains unresolved in the euro area, requiring credible fiscal consolidation.”
The two-year French bond yield rose by nine basis points to 3.64%.
Concerns about France’s instability knocked the euro down to a 17-month low against the pound on Monday morning, when sterling rose to €1.188.

Violence erupted across France after weeks of relatively peaceful demonstrations over conditions in schools and the cost of living, prompting the French president, Emmanuel Macron, to condemn the “unbridled violence” in a televised address on Sunday night.

Tens of thousands of people have attended peaceful marches to demand more teachers and repairs to decrepit schools, but different groups have clashed with police in cities including Paris, Bordeaux, Nice and Marseille.
Jim Reid of Deutsche Bank said the protests “won’t make it easy for the international community to be totally comfortable buying OATs”, referring to French government bonds.
“With France already facing a difficult fiscal backdrop and the 2027 election approaching, the weekend adds another layer of political risk for markets,” he said.
The 30-year bond, which is a benchmark for the French government’s long-term cost of borrowing, rose by ten basis points to 5.46%.
The rises will put further strain on France’s public finances as the government tries to pass a budget for next year to rein in its deficit.
France’s debt-to-GDP stood at 115.6% in 2025, while its budget deficit was 5.1%, compared with 94.3% and 4.3% respectively for the UK.
The unrest adds to “concerns about the political and fiscal troubles in France”, said Neil Wilson, Saxo UK’s investor strategist.
“It underscores how hard it will be for a government to enact the kind of spending restraint required to get the deficit down.”

The French government is preparing a budget that would involve cutting pensions spending and funding for government departments, excluding defence. There are growing fears, however, that political pressure could derail the plans, which could push up borrowing further and add more to the country’s debt pile.
The euro also slipped against the US dollar, down by 0.4% at one stage on Monday to $1.1197.
France’s Cac 40 index, which tracks the biggest companies listed in Paris, fell by 1.4% , compared with a 1.1% drop on the pan-European Stoxx 600 index.
French bank stocks were among the fallers, with Société Générale and BNP Paribas down more than 3%.
Other European stock markets also weakened, with Italy’s FTSE Mib down 1.6% and Spain’s Ibex dropping by 1.9%.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said investors were concerned that higher borrowing costs would increase France’s debt-servicing expenses, reducing its fiscal flexibility at a time when growth is already subdued.

“But France is not alone,” he said. “Spain faces its own political constraints around budgets and fiscal reforms, although stronger economic growth provides some protection, while Italy’s substantial debt stock leaves it particularly sensitive to prolonged periods of elevated yields.”

articles.title: People scour strait of Hormuz for spilt cargo after Iran attacks container ships
articles.summary: At least 15 vessels struck in waterway in past 10 days, with rumours that they were carrying valuable goods
body: People have been scouring the strait of Hormuz for spilt cargo after Iran attacked at least 15 container ships passing through the crucial waterway in the past 10 days.
Some ships have been hit by drones, others by mines. On Sunday, a ship was struck by a rocket-propelled grenade launched from a small boat 75 miles (120km) north-east of the Saudi port of Jubail.

The rise in Iranian attacks appears to have helped resolidify Tehran’s disputed control over the strait, as well as pushing the price of a barrel of Brent crude oil close to $108 a barrel on Monday morning.

Last Wednesday a ship travelling from Karachi, Pakistan, to Fujairah, in the United Arab Emirates, sunk after hitting a mine, according to Iranian state TV. All 21 crew members were evacuated and no injuries were reported. Dozens of its 2,500 containers were seen floating in the water. Rumours that iPhones and other expensive goods were among its cargo – fuelled by fake AI-generated photos published on social media – prompted fishers and others to investigate.
One fisher told an Iranian reporter: “The Arab boatmen, who were closer to the ship, arrived earlier than the Iranians. They used stonecutters to cut the container and took whatever was there.”

Col Javad Mokhtar Rezaei, the deputy head of cultural and social affairs for Iran’s cyber police (Fata), told the Tasnim news agency: “In some cases, the phones offered may actually exist, but exposing electronic components to salt water and extreme humidity can cause corrosion of internal components, damage to the boards, battery and display, and cause hidden malfunctions in the device’s performance.”
Meysam Doost-Mohammadi, a spokesperson for the Iranian mobile phone Aassociation, said it would be unusual for valuable devices to be transported by ship.

The bulk of the recent attacks have occurred close to the coast with Oman, a route that Iran regards as unauthorised. In the seven days to Friday 16 October, 12 vessels were attacked, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO).

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says it has the right to attack any ship that seeks to traverse the strait without its permission or with its transponders off. Officials have also ordered local fishers not to pillage the sea for luxury items, saying the goods are the property of the state.

Two oil tankers were hit on Saturday, including a supertanker carrying 2m barrels of oil, according to the IRGC. The Fars news agency published a video that appears to show the tanker burning, but which cannot be independently verified. A third tanker was hit late on Sunday.

It is disputed how many ships have been hit by mines or IRGC shelling. UKMTO’s weekly overview recorded 254 transits of the strait (125 outbound, 129 inbound) in the week to 14 October, approximately 70% below pre-conflict levels.

Dr Devaraj Asir Ramesh, of Anna University in Chennai, India, warned that the region’s marine habitats faced threats from toxic debris and oil spills, while noise might have disturbed marine life. Iranian strikes on the Emirates, he said, were likely to have contaminated seagrass beds with hydrocarbons and caused auditory damage to cetaceans – marine mammals such as dolphins and porpoises – which are sensitive to loud noise that travels through the sea.

Oil released by attacks on tankers at Fujairah could have caused ecological harm, he added. “Oil spills, chemical leaks and acoustic disturbances have impaired biodiversity, fisheries, aquaculture, desalination, and eco-tourism,” he wrote in the International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Sciences.
On Friday, the Iranian president said the conflicts in Gaza and the wider Middle East had inflicted a significant toll on nature that extended beyond borders and required “international solutions”.

“What has occurred in our region as a result of wars of aggression is ecocide, or environmental genocide, and it must be condemned,” Masoud Pezeshkian said. He argued that countries subjected to economic sanctions or military aggression should not be forced to shoulder the financial burden of environmental damage resulting from conflicts they did not initiate.
Successive studies, mainly by US universities using satellite imagery, have warned of the dangers facing the strait.

Meanwhile, the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, visited Tehran offering to act as an intermediary between Iran and Donald Trump, especially over the issue of Iran’s nuclear stockpile, which the US president insists must be addressed before he lifts his threat to attack Iran again.
Iran has offered to open the strait in six days in return for sanctions relief.

Russia has offered to take Iran’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium, but Iran is reluctant to make a commitment on its nuclear programme and has not given the International Atomic Energy Agency access to its bombed nuclear sites since June 2025. Lavrov also proposed a trilateral summit between China, Russia and Iran to agree new security architecture for the strait. He said the region was on the verge of a full-scale crisis.

Tehran is braced for another attack soon, especially after the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, launched a new national security doctrine on Sunday that included an emphasis on prevention and offence, including pre-emptive strikes on potential threats.

articles.title: Ebola cases in Kenya highlight US failures amid Trump cuts to key services
articles.summary: Opposition to US-led quarantine center in Kenya follows sweeping funding cuts and withdrawal from WHO
body: An eighth person in Kenya has tested positive for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola in the country’s first-ever cluster of cases of the virus, as the second-largest outbreak in history has killed more than 4,300 and sickened more than 9,000 people in the region.

It highlights the diminished role the US has played in the worsening Ebola outbreak by building a controversial quarantine center in Kenya, pulling back health support globally, and banning travelers from certain countries. All of this has also reduced the ability to identify and respond to the outbreak and exacerbated mistrust.

The US created a controversial quarantine center at Kenya’s Laikipia airbase, where Americans returning from the Democratic Republic of the Congo would be required to quarantine. The center, opposed by locals, has stirred distrust in the Kenyan government, leading to protests and a Kenyan court ordering a halt to the center.

“Many Kenyans were concerned about the fact that there was no information and people did not know why the quarantine place was being set up, who was actually going to use it, and what had informed that,” said Allan Maleche, executive director of the Kenya Legal & Ethical Issues Network on HIV and Aids (Kelin). The litigation will be decided in November, he said.
In the meantime, Kenyans were “very cautious around any information that is being given by the government around Ebola”, Maleche said.

Americans who questioned whether the US has the legal authority to quarantine Americans on foreign soil and prevent them from returning home are pushing back against the quarantine center as Kenya faces its first Ebola cases.

“Is this still a viable solution for the US?” asked Jennifer Nuzzo, director of the pandemic center at Brown University school of public health. “Are we posing not only an undue burden on the Kenyan government to be able to handle this, but also is this the safest place to be bringing Americans?”
The US already has “world-class” Ebola treatment units, Nuzzo pointed out.

“American taxpayers built these units for precisely this purpose, and it’s mind-boggling to me that we’re going to leave them empty,” she said. In previous outbreaks, actively ill patients have been evacuated safely to these centers, where they have recovered without further spread of the virus.

The unease follows sweeping cuts to US health support across the world, with the demolition of the US Agency for International Development (USAID) and cuts to funding and staff at health agencies like the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

On 1 October, the CDC closed HIV prevention offices in Angola and South Sudan, with plans to close offices in Zimbabwe. The US has slashed programs across the world – including DR Congo, where the Ebola outbreak is centered, and other countries, like Kenya, bracing for cases as the outbreak widens.
“We have had a lot of concerns after the US first cut funding for HIV promptly without any direction,” Maleche said. “It led to clinics closing. It led to a lot of anxiety among people.”

The US is now negotiating bilateral agreements with each country, including Kenya – a process that has been mired in secrecy, Maleche said. “It’s not very clear what’s the plan, who’s rolling it out, and what will be involved.”

Cuts to decades-long programs mean the affected countries and the US have less insight into what’s happening, in addition to a lessened ability to prevent and stop outbreaks. “When you pull back on those, not only do you leave those countries less prepared to deal with that day-to-day threat, but it also means that they’re less prepared to deal with future emergencies,” Nuzzo said.

The US officially left the World Health Organization (WHO) in January, making it much harder to collaborate on the response to crises like these. When the US left the WHO, it also “pulled out a substantial amount of funding”, said Maleche. That means the WHO’s response had also been “weakened”, he said.

A Kenyan man fell ill in DRC before traveling by road to Uganda and then flying to Nairobi on 3 October, where he died in a hospital two days later. Since then, seven close contacts have tested positive.
Patrick Amoth, the director-general for health, confirmed on Sunday the total number of ‌infections in the country was eight.
Kenya’s ministry of health pointed to the success of contact tracing and quarantine. About 108 people have been quarantined in Nairobi.

“The general feeling is that the contact tracing systems are working,” Maleche said. But Kenyans are also wondering why there were “many lapses” that resulted in a sick person traveling across countries. The border between DR Congo and Uganda has been closed since May. Uganda was declared Ebola-free in August after earlier reporting 20 cases and two deaths.
A French doctor who returned from DR Congo in June tested positive, and several Americans have been evacuated from DR Congo to Europe for Ebola treatment or monitoring.

In Kenya, “the biggest fear is around how will other countries react” to the outbreak, with travel bans a particular worry, Maleche said. The US put travel bans in place from DR Congo and neighboring Uganda and South Sudan once the outbreak was detected in May, but it would be “very ironic” if the US instituted travel bans, given its quarantine center in Kenya, Maleche said.

Raphael Warnock, a Democratic senator from Georgia, and Bill Cassidy, a Republican senator from Louisiana, penned a letter in June to the Senate appropriations committee opposing the Trump administration’s plans to cut back on HIV prevention and monitoring.

Dismantling of USAID, withdrawing from the WHO, and abruptly cutting foreign aid cuts was “degrading our outbreak preparedness” and had “seriously weakened our ability to keep Americans safe from infectious disease”, Warnock said in a statement.

“These cuts to global health funding have led to the erosion of international disease-monitoring infrastructure that helps us catch threats like Ebola before they reach our shores, at a time when the world needs American leadership most.” The US should be strengthening these systems, not abandoning them, he said.

Nuzzo agreed. “It’s about having an understanding of the systems and the conditions in other countries, and eyes and ears in those countries to detect when something out of the ordinary happens, and to get that information as early as possible,” she said. That benefits the US and the countries themselves, she said.

Work such as HIV prevention “can be repurposed”, she added. “You have connections with clinical care, the ability to move medicines, the ability to conduct laboratory tests, the ability to move specimens around – all of those capacities are things that you would use in other disease emergencies.”

articles.title: Albania accused of rushing through Trump-linked resort in formerly protected landscape
